Key Findings

1. AI Automation Risk Is Rising Systematically. The average AI risk score increased from 0.32 (2015–2019 average) to 0.47 (2031–2035 average), a rise of +0.16 points. This trajectory indicates that by 2035, the majority of roles in the dataset face at least moderate automation exposure, with Business Analyst roles at greatest risk (avg score: 0.75).
2. Salary Growth Has Not Kept Pace with Rising Risk. Median salaries shifted from $25,859 (2015–2019) to $37,690 (2031–2035), a +45.7% change. Critically, higher AI risk correlates with lower median salaries (correlation: -0.24), meaning the roles most vulnerable to automation also tend to be less well-compensated — a double exposure for affected workers.
3. Skill Selection Is the Strongest Lever for Job Survival. Java carries the highest average demand score (79.9/100) and is associated with above-average survival rates. Meanwhile, Docker demand has declined most sharply since 2015, signaling waning market relevance.
4. Geography and Experience Create Unequal Exposure. India faces the highest average AI risk (0.40), while UK is least exposed (0.39). Entry-level professionals carry higher automation risk than senior practitioners, widening the experience-risk gap.
5. Job Survival Rates Are Trending Downward. The survival rate (proportion of roles classified as moderate or strong survival) moved from 91.8% (2015–2019) to 86.7% (2031–2035), a change of -5.1% points. Without targeted reskilling, the at-risk workforce segment will continue to expand.

2. AI Automation Risk Landscape

2.1 Risk Score Trends Over Time

The overall average AI risk score across the dataset stands at 0.40. Year-over-year analysis reveals a clear upward trajectory: the score rose from 0.30 in 2015 to 0.51 in 2035, reflecting intensifying automation pressure across all roles and geographies.

Figure 2.1 — Average AI risk score has risen steadily from 2015 to 2035, crossing the medium-risk threshold.

2.2 Risk by Job Title

Business Analyst roles carry the highest average AI risk (0.75), while AI Researcher roles are the least exposed (0.15). The spread between most and least at-risk roles is 0.60 points.

Figure 2.2 — Horizontal ranking of average AI risk scores by job title. Red = high risk; amber = moderate; green = lower risk.
Figure 2.3 — All job titles show rising risk trajectories, but the slope differs by role.

2.3 Risk by Country

Geographic analysis reveals uneven automation exposure. India leads with an average risk of 0.40, while UK is most insulated at 0.39. These differences likely reflect variation in industry composition, AI adoption velocity, and labor market structures.

Figure 2.4 — Average AI risk score by country, revealing geographic disparity in automation exposure.

2.4 Risk by Experience Level

Entry-level professionals face meaningfully higher AI risk than their senior counterparts. This pattern likely reflects the greater routine content in junior roles and the strategic/decision-making components that protect senior positions.

Figure 2.5 — Entry-level roles carry the highest AI risk; senior roles are most insulated.

2.5 Risk Category Distribution Over Time

The proportion of records classified as "High Risk" has expanded over the study period, while "Low Risk" classifications have contracted — a structural shift in the risk landscape.

Figure 2.6 — Stacked area chart showing the proportional shift from low-risk to high-risk classifications over time.

6. Strategic Recommendations

The following recommendations are grounded in the data findings above. Each traces back to a specific insight from this analysis.

  1. Prioritize reskilling toward Java and related high-demand, lower-risk skills. Data shows Java carries the highest average demand score (79.9) and above-average survival rates. Investing reskilling budgets here yields the strongest future-proofing return. (Finding source: Section 4 — Skill Demand & Future-Proofing)
  2. Establish early-warning reskilling programs for Business Analyst and Data Analyst roles. These positions show the highest AI risk scores (0.75 and 0.65 respectively) and are the most likely to face significant automation by 2030. Proactive transition pathways reduce workforce displacement costs. (Finding source: Section 2 — AI Automation Risk Landscape)
  3. Address the salary-risk double exposure. The negative correlation between salary and AI risk (r = -0.24) means workers in the most automation-vulnerable roles also earn the least. Equity-focused reskilling should target these populations first. (Finding source: Section 3.6 — Salary × AI Risk Correlation)
  4. Invest in accelerated career development pathways for entry-level professionals. Entry-level roles carry disproportionately high AI risk compared to senior positions. Mentorship, certification programs, and experience-acceleration initiatives can move workers into more insulated roles faster. (Finding source: Section 2.4 — Risk by Experience Level)
  5. Develop country-specific workforce strategies. India faces 0.01 higher average AI risk than UK. Global reskilling programs should allocate proportionally more resources to high-exposure geographies. (Finding source: Section 2.3 — Risk by Country)
  6. Monitor demand trajectories for Docker and other declining skills. Docker demand has declined by -2.5 points since 2015. Organizations should begin phasing dependency on these skills and redirect training investment toward growth trajectories. (Finding source: Section 4.2 — Skill Demand Trends)
  7. Strengthen education-to-survival pipelines. Data shows that higher education levels correlate with stronger job survival. Expanding access to advanced education — particularly in Java and high-demand domains — is a structural lever for workforce resilience. (Finding source: Section 5.5 — Survival by Education Level)
  8. Use the top survival combinations as talent acquisition blueprints. The highest-survival role-skill-education-geography combinations (e.g., AI Researcher + Deep Learning + Master in USA) should inform hiring and talent development strategy to build inherently resilient teams. (Finding source: Section 5.7 — Top Survival Combinations)

Methodology & Data Notes

This report is based on a synthetic dataset of 12,343 records spanning 2015–2035, covering 10 job titles across 6 countries. All values are derived directly from the source data — no figures have been fabricated or extrapolated beyond what the dataset provides.

Important caveats:

  • Years 2025–2035 represent simulated projections, not observed data. Trends for these years should be interpreted as scenario outputs, not forecasts.
  • Salary values are in USD and do not account for purchasing power parity differences across countries.
  • AI risk scores are model-derived estimates reflecting automation probability, not deterministic outcomes.
  • As a synthetic dataset, the data reflects realistic assumptions but may not capture all real-world complexities.
